statement: Grab Group FY2025 revenue was $3,370m, +20% YoY reported (+18% YoY constant currency), a new annual record.
FY2025 revenue by segment: Deliveries $1,800m (+21% YoY), Mobility $1,219m (+16% YoY), Financial Services $347m (+37% YoY), Others $4m.
FY2025 On-Demand GMV reached an all-time high of $22.1bn (+21% YoY, +19% cc): Deliveries GMV $14.24bn (+21% YoY), Mobility GMV $7.90bn (+19% YoY).
FY2025 Group Adjusted EBITDA was $500m (margin 14.8% of revenue), up $187m YoY from $313m in FY2024; Total Segment Adjusted EBITDA was $868m.

FY2025 Segment Adjusted EBITDA: Deliveries $287m (2.0% of GMV, +35bps YoY), Mobility $690m (8.7% of GMV, +21% YoY), Financial Services -$110m (loss widened 5% YoY on higher credit-loss provisions), Others $1m; regional corporate costs were $368m (vs $350m FY2024).

Grab's economic engine is a two-speed model: a high-frequency, low-take-rate Mobility business generating structural profit (8.7% EBITDA/GMV) that cross-subsidizes a scale-chasing Deliveries business only recently turning modestly profitable (2.0% EBITDA/GMV), while Financial Services remains a deliberate, credit-risk-funded loss center building toward optionality value (lending book, deposits, insurance) rather than near-term earnings.

Group take rate (revenue / On-Demand GMV) was approximately 15.2% in FY2025 ($3,019m On-Demand-attributable revenue proxy / $22,138m GMV, ex-Financial Services and Others revenue), broadly stable versus FY2024, indicating monetization gains are coming mainly from GMV growth and advertising attach rather than higher core take rates.

Deliveries Adjusted EBITDA margin improvement is increasingly advertising-led: Deliveries revenue growth (+21% YoY) outpaced Deliveries GMV growth (+21% YoY, in line) while margin expanded 35bps, and Grab explicitly attributes the gain to 'growing contributions from our Advertising business and gains in operating leverage'; quarterly active self-serve advertisers were up 21% YoY to 228,000 with average spend per advertiser up 23% YoY in Q4 2025.

Advertising (embedded in Deliveries revenue/EBITDA, not separately disclosed as a line item) is treated as the single highest-operating-leverage, highest-incremental-margin lever within Grab's model because it monetizes existing GMV/attention without incremental driver, rider or merchant-partner incentive cost.

Grab issued $1.5bn of convertible notes in FY2025 (proceeds recognized in financing cash flows); the conversion feature is an IFRS derivative liability re-measured every period, adding non-cash fair-value volatility to reported profit/loss ($34m net gain in FY2025) without affecting Adjusted EBITDA or underlying cash flow.

Grab is structurally a net-cash, rate-beneficiary business at the group level: FY2025 net finance income was $203m (finance income $240m vs finance costs $71m) on ~$5.4bn net cash liquidity, so a further 100bp move in USD and SGD/MYR/IDR short rates has a direct, disclosed P&L effect via interest income on cash/time deposits, partially offset by funding-cost sensitivity in the growing digital-bank loan/deposit book.

A 100bp decline in USD/regional policy rates from current levels would reduce Grab's annualized net finance income by an estimated $50-55m (roughly proportional to the ~$5.4bn net cash liquidity base), modestly pressuring reported (though not Adjusted EBITDA) profitability, while lowering GXS/GXBank funding costs and supporting loan-book net interest margin.
notes: Approximate sensitivity; Grab does not disclose an explicit duration or rate-sensitivity table, so this is a judgmental order-of-magnitude estimate, not a company-guided figure.

statement: Grab's revenue and costs are almost entirely denominated in ASEAN local currencies (IDR, MYR, THB, VND, PHP) while it reports in USD, so reported growth is systematically noisier than underlying constant-currency growth; management-disclosed FX drag was ~1-2pp on FY2025 revenue growth (18% cc vs 20% reported... note reported was actually higher than cc, implying regional currencies appreciated versus USD in FY2025) and Maybank flagged a further 3-4pp FX headwind to Q3 2026 reported GMV growth, indicating a reversal (regional currency weakness) intra-2026.

Fuel-price inflation directly compresses driver-partner economics in Mobility and Deliveries (two-wheel/car delivery); Q2 2026 management specifically cited 'elevated fuel prices' as a headwind to driver supply/economics even as MTUs hit a record, implying Grab may need to raise partner incentives to protect driver retention if fuel costs stay elevated, pressuring Mobility's 8.6-8.7% EBITDA/GMV margin.

The macro-transmission thesis (net cash position as a rate tailwind, local-currency cost base as a natural hedge) would be falsified if net finance income declines materially faster than net cash liquidity implies (signaling deteriorating yield or FX losses) or if a sustained USD-strength cycle against ASEAN currencies pushes constant-currency vs reported growth spreads persistently negative by more than the ~3-4pp already flagged for Q3 2026.

Grab holds an estimated ~54-55% share of the Southeast Asian food-delivery market by 2025 GMV (Nikkei Asia survey), with Foodpanda a distant #2 at ~11-16% regionally (but #2 with 22-24% share in Singapore and Malaysia specifically), ShopeeFood ~9-12%, and Gojek(GoTo) ~10%.

Grab's ride-hailing share is regionally dominant but geographically uneven: >95% in Malaysia, and estimated ~70% across combined SEA Mobility GMV, but GoTo/Gojek retains an estimated majority (~60%) of Indonesian ride-hailing, Grab's single largest market by population and GMV potential.
notes: Cross-country share estimates vary materially by source methodology (GMV vs rides vs app downloads); treat as directional, not precise.

statement: Deliveroo's exit from Singapore in March 2026 (vacating ~7% share) is a near-term tailwind for Grab/Foodpanda consolidation, but the more consequential structural variable is Foodpanda's own ownership: Delivery Hero has signaled willingness to sell/exit Southeast Asia, and a ShopeeFood (Sea Ltd) acquisition would combine Foodpanda with Sea's e-commerce/payments/logistics ecosystem into a much stronger #2, while a Meituan acquisition would import an operator with far deeper food-delivery execution experience than either.

Pricing-power stress test: Grab has demonstrated an ability to raise Deliveries and Mobility segment margins (2.0% and 8.7% of GMV respectively in FY2025, both up YoY) simultaneously with GMV growth of 19-21%, i.e., margin expansion has not required volume or share sacrifice to date -- a genuine (if early) pricing-power signal in a two-sided marketplace with real switching costs (loyalty/points, saved payment methods, super-app bundling). However, this test has not yet been run against renewed, well-funded competitive discounting (see VC-03), which is the scenario Maybank models as cutting 2030 Deliveries EBITDA by 23-41%.

Driver-partners (labor input) are Grab's most politically and commercially contested 'supplier': Vietnam's National Competition Commission opened a review of Grab's fare-setting, commission and fee/deduction policies in September 2026 after drivers called for a weekend work stoppage, directly testing whether Grab can sustain current commission/take-rate levels in one of its larger Mobility/Deliveries markets without regulatory intervention.

Margin compression in a renewed Deliveries price war would land primarily on Grab and Foodpanda's respective P&Ls (via consumer/partner incentives) rather than on restaurant/merchant-partners or consumers, based on FY2025 behavior where incentives grew (partner incentives +33% YoY, consumer incentives +17% YoY) roughly in line with or ahead of GMV growth even in a benign competitive year -- meaning incentive intensity, not commission rates, is the primary lever competitors would pull, and the primary variable to monitor for margin risk.

No independent, audited third-party market-share dataset was accessed in this pass; all Deliveries/Mobility share figures rely on survey-based secondary press (Nikkei) and a single sell-side note (Maybank via TechNode). A subscription-grade data source (e.g., Momentum Works, Measurable AI) would materially improve confidence in the value-chain/competitive module.

Capital cycle position: Grab is past the 'land grab' capacity-building phase (heavy cash burn, negative EBITDA through FY2023) and is now in an early harvest phase -- 18 consecutive quarters of Adjusted EBITDA growth through Q2 2026, first full-year net profit in FY2025, and a $500m-then-$750m-expanded buyback signaling management confidence that reinvestment needs are moderating relative to cash generation.

Leading indicator set for cycle position: (1) Segment Adjusted EBITDA margin trend -- Deliveries 2.0% FY2025 vs 1.65% FY2024 (implied from $196m/$11,723m), improving; (2) MTU growth -- 14% YoY FY2025, decelerating slightly from FY2024's 16% YoY off a larger base but still double-digit; (3) Incentive intensity -- consumer incentives grew slower than GMV in FY2025 (17% vs 21%), a bullish signal on competitive discipline; (4) Loan portfolio growth -- +120% YoY, an aggressive re-acceleration of risk-taking in Financial Services that is the opposite signal (capacity expansion, not harvest) within that sub-segment.

Permanent-impairment test on Financial Services: the segment's widening Adjusted EBITDA loss (-$110m FY2025 vs -$105m FY2024, +5% worse) is classified as cyclical/deliberate rather than structural impairment, because it is explicitly driven by credit-loss provisioning that scales with a loan book growing 120% YoY (i.e., a growth-investment choice with a plausible path to segment profitability as the book seasons and NPLs stabilize 'well within risk appetite' per management), not a sign of unviable unit economics. This conclusion should be revisited if 90-day NPL ratios or provisioning rates rise materially.

Grab does not disclose segment-level 90-day non-performing loan (NPL) ratios, loan-loss coverage ratios, or a cohort-level view of loan-book seasoning; management's assertion that NPLs are 'well within risk appetite' cannot be independently verified from public disclosure. This is a material gap for underwriting the Financial Services impairment-vs-cyclical call in CS-03.

Overall cycle-vs-structure conclusion: Mixed. Deliveries and Mobility show structural margin improvement consistent with maturing marketplace economics and genuine operating leverage; Financial Services shows a structural (not cyclical) strategic choice to prioritize loan-book scale over near-term profitability, which is rational if unit economics hold but is a real source of estimate risk given disclosure limitations (CS-04).

Q2 2026: Group revenue $997m (+22% YoY, +21% cc); Adjusted EBITDA $168m (+54% YoY, margin 16.9% vs 13.3% prior year); this was the 18th consecutive quarter of Adjusted EBITDA growth; net income $235m vs $20m prior year; MTUs hit a record 53.9m (+17% YoY).

Q2 2026 segment detail: Deliveries revenue $531m (+21% YoY) / EBITDA $96m (+53% YoY, 2.3% of GMV); Mobility revenue $331m (+12% YoY) / EBITDA $191m (+16% YoY, 8.6% of GMV); Financial Services revenue $134m (+59% YoY) / EBITDA -$15m (improved from -$26m); gross loan portfolio $2.318bn (+197% YoY). FY2026 guidance raised to revenue $4.10-4.15bn (22-23% growth) and Adjusted EBITDA $720-740m (44-48% growth), up from prior $4.04-4.10bn / $700-720m, citing core momentum plus consolidation of SuperBank and Stash.

Balance sheet as of Dec 31, 2025: total assets $11,983m; cash and cash equivalents $3,433m; total equity $6,757m; total liabilities $5,226m, including $1,680m current loans/borrowings (reflecting the $1.5bn convertible-note issuance) and $1,629m customer deposits from the banking business. Gross cash liquidity $7.4bn; net cash liquidity $5.4bn.

Share count as of Dec 31, 2025: 3,969m Class A + 120m Class B ordinary shares outstanding; weighted-average basic shares FY2025 were 4,092m; FY2025 diluted EPS was $0.06 (basic $0.07), versus a diluted/basic loss of $(0.03) in FY2024. As of Jun 30, 2026: 3,974m Class A + 105m Class B outstanding.

Base-case FY2026 forecast adopts the midpoint of Grab's raised guidance: revenue $4,125m (+22.4% YoY) and Adjusted EBITDA $730m (17.7% margin), consistent with the company's own guided range and with sell-side consensus revenue of ~$4.19bn (slightly above the guided range, reflecting some analysts modeling upside from SuperBank/Stash consolidation).

Base-case FY2027E/FY2028E revenue growth assumed to decelerate gradually from ~22% (FY2026) to ~17% (FY2027) to ~15% (FY2028) as the business scales and constant-currency GMV growth normalizes toward regional on-demand-economy growth rates (high-teens), consistent with management's own '2025-2028 Group Revenue 20% CAGR' guidance (which implies some years above and some below 20%).

Base-case Adjusted EBITDA is assumed to reach management's explicit 2028 target of $1.5bn, implying roughly $1.0-1.05bn in FY2027E (bridging from the $730m FY2026E base) and $1.5bn in FY2028E; this requires continued Deliveries/Mobility margin expansion (base case: Deliveries reaching ~3.0% of GMV and Mobility ~9.5% of GMV by FY2028E) more than offsetting a still-loss-making but narrowing Financial Services segment.
notes: This is management's own long-range target, not an independently derived bottom-up build; treat FY2027E as an interpolation, not a disclosed figure.

statement: Adjusted Free Cash Flow conversion assumed to rise from 58% in FY2025 ($290m/$500m) toward management's 80% target by FY2028, implying FY2026E Adjusted FCF of ~$460-480m (consistent with TTM trend of $450m disclosed at Q2 2026) and FY2028E Adjusted FCF of ~$1.2bn.

Reported net income (FY2025 $200m; Q2 2026 $235m) is meaningfully flattered by non-operating items that are volatile and not part of the core operating thesis: FY2025 included $203m net finance income (mostly interest income on the large cash pile plus a $34m non-cash fair-value gain on the convertible-note derivative) against only $65m of IFRS operating profit. A normalization of interest rates lower, or a reversal of the derivative fair-value gain, would compress reported net income far more than it would affect Adjusted EBITDA.

SuperBank (Indonesia digital bank, majority-owned via Grab/Singtel/Emtek consortium) and Stash consolidation into Grab's reported Financial Services segment, cited explicitly as a driver of the Q2 2026 guidance raise, is a measurable near-term catalyst: watch for FY2026 Financial Services revenue growth materially exceeding the FY2025 37% YoY pace and for disclosed loan-portfolio/deposit growth in Indonesia specifically.

As of Sept 13, 2026: GRAB share price ~$3.05, market capitalization ~$12.4bn (implied ~4.08bn total Class A + Class B shares), 52-week range $2.96-$6.62 (i.e., trading near the 52-week low, roughly 54% below the 52-week high).

Enterprise value approximated as market cap less net cash liquidity: $12,440m - $5,400m (Q2 2026 net cash liquidity) = ~$7,040m. This likely understates true EV modestly to the extent the $5.4bn net cash liquidity figure already nets out the $1.5bn convertible notes as 'loans and borrowings' while the equity value of the conversion option is not separately added back; treated as a reasonable approximation, not a precise EV build.

At the approximated EV of ~$7.0bn, GRAB trades at roughly 1.7x EV/FY2026E Revenue (guidance midpoint $4,125m) and roughly 9.6x EV/FY2026E Adjusted EBITDA (guidance midpoint $730m); on FY2025 actuals, this is ~2.1x EV/Sales and ~14.1x EV/Adjusted EBITDA.

Peer comps (approximate, mixed methodologies -- see sources for caveats): Uber ~14.8x EV/EBITDA, ~2.7x EV/Revenue, ~16.7% revenue growth; DoorDash ~54x EV/EBITDA; Meituan ~9.5x EV/EBITDA (CY2026 consensus), ~5.6% Q1 2026 revenue growth (China price-war-affected); GoTo ~15.1x EV/EBITDA, ~15% revenue growth, ~$3bn market cap; Sea Limited ~27.5x EV/EBITDA (different scope/methodology), ~36% FY2025 revenue growth.

Grab's ~9.6x forward EV/EBITDA sits below Uber's ~14.8x despite comparable or higher forecast Adjusted EBITDA growth (Grab guided 44-48% FY2026 growth vs Uber's ~17% revenue growth and decelerating EBITDA growth), and below GoTo's ~15.1x despite Grab's structurally superior segment economics (profitable Mobility, near-breakeven Deliveries, dominant regional share) versus GoTo's smaller scale and heavier Indonesia-only mix. This gap is only partially explained by index/passive-flow effects (GRAB is a US-listed EM-adjacent small/mid-cap) and Financial-Services execution risk; it is a candidate variant-perception source (see final synthesis) rather than proof of mispricing on its own.

Reverse-expectations read: at ~9.6x EV/FY2026E EBITDA and a share price 54% below its 52-week high, the market is pricing something closer to Maybank's 'moderate-to-aggressive competitive intensity' scenario for Deliveries (23-41% cut to 2030 EBITDA versus base case) than a clean continuation of the current 18-quarter EBITDA-growth streak toward the $1.5bn 2028 target; the price appears to embed meaningful skepticism about (a) durability of Deliveries margin gains against Foodpanda/ShopeeFood consolidation risk and (b) Financial Services ever reaching breakeven, rather than crediting company guidance at face value.

Bear-case valuation scenario: Deliveries EBITDA/GMV margin stalls at ~2.0-2.2% (competitive re-intensification per Maybank's aggressive scenario), Mobility margin holds near 8.5-9.0% (structurally protected, less contested), Financial Services losses widen further on credit normalization, and FY2028 Group Adjusted EBITDA reaches only ~$950m-$1.05bn (vs. $1.5bn target) at a compressed ~7-8x forward EV/EBITDA multiple given confirmed competitive erosion.

Bull-case valuation scenario: Deliveries margin expands to ~3.5-4.0% of GMV on continued advertising penetration and benign competition (Foodpanda exits or is acquired by a disciplined operator), Mobility expands toward 9.5-10%, Financial Services reaches segment breakeven by FY2028 as the loan book seasons, Group Adjusted EBITDA reaches or exceeds the $1.5bn 2028 target with FCF conversion at or above 80%, supporting a re-rating toward peer-average ~12-14x forward EV/EBITDA.

The single variable with the largest valuation delta across scenarios is the Deliveries segment Adjusted EBITDA margin trajectory (2.0% FY2025 actual vs. a 1.5-4.0% bear-to-bull range by FY2028), because Deliveries is both Grab's largest-GMV segment and its most competitively contested; a 100bp swing in Deliveries EBITDA/GMV margin on an estimated ~$20-24bn FY2028E Deliveries GMV base is worth roughly $200-240m of Group Adjusted EBITDA, larger than the entire bear-to-base delta in Financial Services losses.

The 'Reasonable/Depressed' valuation-expectations classification (VAL-06) would be falsified toward 'Demanding' if GRAB re-rates to peer-average multiples (12-14x forward EV/EBITDA) without a corresponding acceleration in segment fundamentals, or would be confirmed/strengthened toward 'Depressed' if Deliveries margin continues expanding through at least two more quarters without competitive share loss, at which point the multiple gap to Uber/GoTo would represent a clearer mispricing rather than a rational discount for competitive/regulatory risk.

Investment regime classification: Structural Growth with Mid-Cycle profitability inflection. Supporting datapoints: (1) 18 consecutive quarters of Adjusted EBITDA growth through Q2 2026; (2) first full-year net profit in FY2025 after a 13-year cash-burn history; (3) FY2026 guidance raised mid-year (revenue and EBITDA both raised at Q2), indicating positive, not merely stable, momentum.

6-12 month earnings-revision risk: Positive. Dominant driver is continued Deliveries advertising monetization and Mobility operating leverage, reinforced by the Q2 2026 guidance raise attributing upside partly to SuperBank/Stash consolidation (an M&A-driven revenue add that consensus may not yet fully reflect).

Bull catalyst: two consecutive quarters of Deliveries Adjusted EBITDA/GMV margin expansion (from the current 2.0-2.3% level) without a corresponding deceleration in Deliveries GMV growth below ~18% YoY, confirming pricing power holds even as Foodpanda's ownership situation resolves.

Bear risk: a confirmed adverse outcome from the Vietnam National Competition Commission review of Grab's commission/fare policies (e.g., a mandated cap on commission rates or forced fare-setting transparency) that is replicated or referenced by regulators in Indonesia, Philippines or Thailand, given Vietnam's history as a bellwether for ASEAN gig-economy regulation.

Key monitor for next quarter (Q3 2026): Deliveries Segment Adjusted EBITDA margin (% of GMV). Current value 2.3% (Q2 2026). Expected direction: management guidance implies continued gradual improvement. Bull threshold: >=2.5% with GMV growth sustained >=18% YoY cc. Bear threshold: <2.0% or GMV growth cc decelerating below 15% YoY, either of which would signal renewed competitive intensity per the Maybank scenario framework.

Variant perception #1: Consensus view is that Grab's discount to Uber/GoTo multiples reflects fair compensation for Financial Services losses and competitive risk. Variant view: the discount is too large given Grab's regional category leadership and superior segment-level margin structure in its two largest segments; evidence needed is 2-3 more quarters of Deliveries margin resilience against Foodpanda; investment consequence is a re-rating catalyst if evidence confirms, or validation of the discount if Deliveries margin stalls.

Variant perception #2: Consensus (per Maybank and broad sell-side 'Strong Buy' rating with $5.86 average PT, implying ~92% upside from the $3.05 price) appears to treat the GXS/GXBank/SuperBank digital-banking build-out as a call option with limited downside. Variant view: the -$110m FY2025 Financial Services Adjusted EBITDA loss plus GXS Group's separately-reported S$208m FY2025 loss (S006) represents a larger, more persistent capital draw than headline Group Adjusted EBITDA suggests, since GXS's regulatory capital needs sit partly outside Grab's consolidated Financial Services segment disclosure; evidence needed is clearer disclosure of capital injected into/consolidated from GXS Group and SuperBank; investment consequence is downside to the 2028 Adjusted EBITDA target if capital calls or loss-sharing exceed current run-rate assumptions.

Alpha map: (1) Deliveries advertising monetization -- market awareness Medium, earnings impact Medium-High, probability High, monitor = quarterly active advertiser count/spend. (2) Foodpanda ownership resolution -- market awareness Medium (covered by sell-side), earnings impact High, probability Medium (12-24mo), monitor = Delivery Hero corporate actions/SEA press. (3) Vietnam regulatory outcome -- market awareness Low-Medium (just broke Sept 2026), earnings impact Medium (Vietnam is a mid-sized market), probability Medium, monitor = National Competition Commission rulings. (4) Grab-GoTo combination -- market awareness High (repeatedly rumored), earnings impact Very High if realized, probability Low-Medium, monitor = Indonesian regulatory/Danantara developments.

Driver/partner classification and gig-economy labor regulation risk: Grab classifies driver-partners as independent contractors across ASEAN; a shift toward employee-style classification in any major market (Indonesia, Vietnam, Philippines, Thailand) would raise costs (minimum wage, benefits, social security contributions) and could force pricing or commission changes with limited ability to pass costs through given competitive intensity.

Uber Technologies holds an estimated ~13.5% stake in Grab (a legacy of Uber's 2018 SEA market exit/sale to Grab); this concentrated strategic holding is a persistent secondary-sale overhang risk that can pressure the share price independent of operating fundamentals if Uber elects to monetize the position.

Dual-class share structure (Class A / Class B ordinary shares, 3,974m / 105m respectively as of Q2 2026) concentrates voting control with insiders/founders, which can misalign minority-shareholder governance influence over major strategic decisions such as a potential GoTo combination or further capital allocation choices (buybacks vs. Financial Services capital injections).

Credit risk in the rapidly scaling loan book: gross loan portfolio grew from $536m (Q4 2024) to $1,180m (Q4 2025, net) to $2,318m (Q2 2026, gross), a sustained triple-digit YoY growth rate; even 'well within risk appetite' NPLs on a book growing this fast can deteriorate quickly if regional consumer credit conditions weaken, and the segment's provisioning already drives most of its -$110m to -$25m/quarter Adjusted EBITDA losses.

Continued execution against the raised FY2026 guidance ($4.10-4.15bn revenue, $720-740m Adjusted EBITDA) at each remaining quarterly print (Q3 2026, Q4 2026) is the most immediate, measurable catalyst; a beat-and-raise pattern (as occurred at Q2 2026) would reinforce the 18-consecutive-quarter EBITDA growth narrative and could compress the valuation gap to peers.

Resolution (in either direction) of persistent Grab-GoTo merger speculation would be a high-magnitude catalyst: a combination would materially reduce Indonesian competitive intensity in both Mobility and Deliveries (Grab's largest addressable but currently GoTo-led ride-hailing market) and could re-rate the stock on synergy/consolidation logic, while a definitive, credible denial that ends the speculation cycle would remove an M&A-integration-risk overhang that some investors may currently be pricing.

FY2022 financial figures (revenue $1,433m, Adjusted EBITDA -$793m, net loss $1,740m) are sourced only from a secondary web-search aggregation (S005), not independently confirmed against Grab's FY2022 Form 20-F. These figures are used for long-run trend context only (data/historical-financials.csv, marked with source_id S005) and should not be treated with the same confidence as FY2023-FY2026 figures, which are corroborated by primary filings (S002, S003, S004).

This workspace does not have access to Grab's full Form 20-F risk-factor disclosure, related-party transaction detail (notably GXS Group/SuperBank consolidation mechanics and any capital commitments), or segment-level balance sheet data (assets/liabilities by segment). A follow-on research pass incorporating the FY2025 20-F (once filed) would materially strengthen the Financial Services and balance-sheet-risk analysis.

No independent DCF-grade regional macro dataset (ASEAN GDP growth, urbanization, e-commerce/on-demand-economy TAM forecasts) was ingested in this pass; TAM/penetration assumptions embedded in the valuation module rely on management commentary and sell-side scenario framing (Maybank) rather than a primary macro/industry-data source (e.g., Google-Temasek-Bain e-Conomy SEA report, which was not accessed here).

The FY2023 and FY2022 Adjusted EBITDA loss figures embed different cost-adjustment methodologies over time as Grab has periodically revised its non-IFRS reconciliation (e.g., the 2025 reclassification of M&A costs previously bundled into legal/tax/regulatory settlement provisions, disclosed as a comparative restatement in S002). Historical Adjusted EBITDA figures pre-FY2024 should be treated as approximately, not perfectly, comparable to current-methodology figures.
